title: Model Photos Without a Photoshoot | AIVideosUGC
description: Get model photos without a photoshoot: photograph the garment flat, pick an adult look and setting, then check the fit before posting. Learn how and try it.
h1: How to Get Model Photos Without a Photoshoot
lead: A flat photo of the garment can become a picture of an adult wearing it. Check the fit details before you post.
secondary_keywords: on-model photos from a flat lay
summary: A flat or hanger photo becomes an adult wearing the piece. Check the neckline, length, print, and zippers before you post.

paras: When a flat photo is enough, how to shoot the garment, and how to save a look. Jewelry, what to compare, a full color set, three steps, and the other photo tools.
sections.alt: Adult man with short silver hair wearing a plain gray hoodie outside a storefront.

sections.h2: Put the Piece on an AI Model
paras: A Tuesday drop of six coats can go up while the sewer is still finishing the last hem. You do not need a person in the room to wear them that morning.
A photo of the coat on the table is the source. You choose an adult and a room, and the coat appears on that person. The image can help a shopper see the collar.
sections.alt: Adult woman with short copper hair wearing a plain gray hoodie on an autumn city sidewalk.

sections.h2: Photograph the Garment Before the Drop
paras: Once a flat photo exists, the arrival can go on an adult without a studio booking. Lay the piece flat, or hang it on a bare wall, shoot it from the front in daylight, and steam the wrinkles out first.

Creases in that photo can turn into odd folds on the person. Get the whole garment in the frame, including the sleeves, the hem, and the collar. Turn a print toward the camera. Photograph each color on its own. A generated color may not match the real garment. For photos that are not on a person, the [photo tools](page:photo-hub) cover other angles and close details.
sections.alt: Hands smooth a plain gray hoodie beside a wooden hanger on a light surface.

sections.h2: One Saved Face for the Set
paras: The next piece keeps the same face, so the set looks like one shoot. Name the person once, the way you would name a house model.

Put that saved person on the [marketplace listing](page:plat-amazon) and on an [Instagram post](page:plat-instagram), not only on your own product page. A ring and a pair of glasses can use the same person as the skirt. A hoodie might be a young man by a brick wall, hands in the front pocket, in cloudy daylight. A request for a celebrity, or for someone meant to look like a famous person, may be refused. On the product page, put a plain product photo first, then the photos of the piece being worn.

sections.h2: Can Jewelry Use the Same Path?
paras: Yes. Use a close, sharp photo of the piece on a plain surface. Keep the clasp, the stones, and the chain easy to see. Save the look if the next piece should be on the same person.

A short line is enough. Try a close side view, hair back, soft window light, and the earring easy to see. In the result, count the stones and check the clasp. See whether a necklace hangs where that length should. Small pieces need a sharper photo than clothing does.
A shopper can see that the linen dress falls to the ankle and that the stripe stays on the hip. That is a picture, not a promise that a size medium will fit them. Keep the size chart on the listing.

Compare each image with the real piece. Check the neckline, the sleeve and hem length, where the print sits, the number of buttons, and which side the zipper is on. Stripes and plaid should line up the way they do on the garment. Give the hands and the hairline a second look. If anything does not match, make a new version. Plan two or three images per piece: one full view, one closer photo of the cloth or the stone, and one in a setting that fits how it is worn. Files come out square, which fits a product gallery. For a feed post, [ad images](page:social-ad-photos) can turn a photo you already reviewed into a square ad image. If you sell the dress to women in their forties, pick that person.
sections.alt: Adult East Asian man checking the sleeve and hem of a plain gray hoodie in a fitting room.

sections.h2: Make the Whole Color Set Together
paras: When one arrival has more than one color, run them together with the same saved look and the same scene. Review every file before it goes on the site.

Pair the worn photos with a flat photo from the [photo tools](page:photo-hub). Add a room scene from [lifestyle photos](page:lifestyle-photos). Add a plain backdrop from the [background tool](page:change-background). A new color belongs on the [color variant](page:tpl-color) page. Compare it with the real garment before you use it. [Fashion listings](page:ind-fashion-clothing) can use the same saved look across the collection.

sections.h2: How to Make Model Photos in 3 Steps
paras: Steam the shirt and photograph it so the collar and both sleeves are in the frame. A hanger against a bare wall works. A photo of someone already wearing it works too.
Decide the room before the pose. A kitchen stool reads differently from a white wall. The shirt still comes from your photo, and you can save that person for the next color.
Download the image. Square fits the gallery. Choose a tall or wide frame when the channel asks for it. Then check the neckline, length, print, and zippers against the real piece.

faq.q: How does a photo of someone wearing the piece get made?
faq.a: Photograph the garment so the whole piece is in frame, choose the person you saved, and look at the collar before you download.

faq.q: Can I put my own products on a generated face?
faq.a: Yes. The garment in the picture is yours. You choose who wears it.

faq.q: Will the same person appear in all my photos?
faq.a: Only when you pick the saved person again. A new description can grow a different face. Keep a note of the hair so the next piece matches the first.

faq.q: How close is this to a studio shoot?
faq.a: It puts the garment on a person in a room you name. Check the neckline, length, print, and zippers.

faq.q: Can a catalog send these photos through the API?
faq.a: Yes. A catalog can send products through the API and get the photos back.

faq.q: Do I need to say the person in the photo is generated?
faq.a: Check the current disclosure rule for the site where the image will appear. Rules differ and they change, so follow the current one.

faq.q: What photo should I start from?
faq.a: Use a sharp, front-facing photo with the whole garment visible. Smooth wrinkles and use even light so fabric, print, and trim are easy to review.

faq.q: Can AI model photos show how a garment fits?
faq.a: No. It cannot show how a size will sit on a shopper. Keep your size chart and measurements on the listing.

faq.q: How many credits does one on-model photo use?
faq.a: One photo uses 24 credits. The cost shows before you start. If it fails, the credits come back.

faq.q: Can I use jewelry as well as clothing?
faq.a: Yes. Start with a close photo that shows the clasp, stones, and chain, then check those details in the result.

faq.q: How should I review the result?
faq.a: Compare it with the real piece. Check the neckline, sleeve and hem length, print position, buttons, zipper side, clasp, stones, hands, and hairline.

faq.q: Can I make all the colors together?
faq.a: Yes. Save the look and run the colors in one go. Review each file. A generated color may not match the real garment, so compare them.
